To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

African American college students (and, in part, White college students as well) encouraged to view their intelligence as malleably improvable obtained higher grades than their counterparts in control conditions.
African American college students' grades are improved by encouraging them to view intelligence as a malleability, rather than as a fixed trait.

African American college students who were encouraged to view intelligence the object of stereotype threat as malleable, as opposed to fixed, reported greater enjoyment of academics and greater engagement with academics, and obtained higher grades than African American students in two comparison conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the psychological and academic effects of stereotype threat on African American college students.
the psychological mechanisms by which stereotypes can undermine the performance and psychological engagement of students.
the effects of stereotype threat on academic performance and psychological disengagement from academics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
encouraging students to view intelligence as a malleability rather than a fixed capacity may be a promising method for reducing the impact of negative stereotypes on African American students.
this study demonstrates the potential of a relatively simple, inexpensive intervention to help African American students overcome the negative effects of stereotype threat.
encouraging students to view intelligence as a malleability can help them resist the detrimental effects of stereotype threat.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of negative stereotypes on academic performance and psychological well-being can be mitigated by encouraging students to view the intellectual abilities targeted by these stereotypes as malleable rather that fixed.

African American students who are encouraged to view intelligence in a malleable fashion will be less likely to experience the detrimental effects of stereotypes on their academic performance and psychological well being.
the effects of stereotype threat on African American college students can be reduced by encouraging them to view intelligence as an object of effort.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way students are encouraged to view intelligence can have important consequences for their academic performance.
African American students' grades can be improved by teaching them to think about intelligence in a way that is more consistent with the stereotype that threatens them.
the malleability of intelligence can be used as a resource to help students resist stereotype threat and its effects.
